messages.content:
Marcus: ok lads stag do. Prague. done. booked.
Jonno: nothing is booked marcus you sent a link
Dev: I can't do Prague my passport ran out in 2019
Marcus: then RENEW IT
Dev: it takes six weeks
Jonno: stag is in four

Hold it, all three of you. Marcus, a link in a group chat is not a booking, it's a wish with a URL. Dev, your passport expired during a previous decade and you're only mentioning it now, which tells me everything about how you run your affairs. Jonno, you're the only one doing arithmetic, so congratulations, you're now the treasurer. Four weeks, one man with no passport. Prague is dead. Bury it, say a few words, move on.

Marcus: so where then
Jonno: Newcastle?
Dev: Newcastle in November is just Prague with worse odds of survival
Marcus: what about Bournemouth
Jonno: who goes to Bournemouth for a stag

Bournemouth's a seaside town that goes to bed at nine with a cocoa and a grievance. Newcastle, on the other hand, is a city built entirely to receive groups of men in matching shirts and send them home lighter. Dev, it's cold, yes. Wear a coat. You're not a delicate orchid, you're a man who let a passport lapse for half a decade. Newcastle. Train, not car, nobody wants to be designated driver on a stag. Jonno, get prices for a Friday and Saturday night.

Jonno: ok train is £74 return each, apartment sleeps 8 is £640 for 2 nights
Marcus: that's well cheap
Dev: who's actually coming tho, it was 8 then it was 6
Marcus: Kieran's coming
Jonno: Kieran said maybe
Marcus: maybe is yes for Kieran

Maybe is not yes for anyone, Marcus. Maybe is a man keeping his options open in case something better turns up, and Kieran has been 'maybe' since primary school. Here's how this goes: Jonno puts a deposit request in the chat. Forty quid each, by Friday. Money in, you're coming. No money, you're a rumour. You'll have your real headcount in four days without anyone having to have a feelings conversation.

Dev: forty quid sent
Marcus: sent
Jonno: Kieran's left the group chat
Marcus: he's probably just reinstalling whatsapp

Nobody reinstalls WhatsApp at the exact moment money's requested, Marcus. That's not a software issue, that's a character issue. Kieran's made his choice and he's made it quietly, which is the most Kieran way to do anything. Wish him well, and book the apartment for seven, with the sofa bed as a spare in case his conscience wakes up.

Marcus: fine. but I'm still doing matching shirts
Dev: absolutely not
Jonno: depends what's on them

Marcus, you can have shirts. But the groom's face goes on the front, and something he said that he'll regret goes on the back, and Dev gets veto on the wording. That's not a compromise, that's governance. Now go and tell the groom he's going to Newcastle before one of you lets slip Prague and he starts learning Czech.

Tash: Canberra. It's Canberra.
Owen: it's Sydney, everyone knows it's Sydney
Bex: I'm with Owen tbh
Tash: you two are going to lose us this quiz
Owen: Sydney has the opera house, it's obviously the capital

Owen, that's like saying the capital of England is Blackpool because it's got a tower. Canberra. Tash is right and has been right this whole time while you two outvoted her on vibes. Write it down, Tash, and from now on, any geography question, she holds the pen. Bex, I'll be generous and assume you were just being loyal. Don't be loyal. Be correct. Loyalty doesn't win the meat raffle.

Hannah: CODE RED he's coming up the road
Liam: he's not meant to be back till 7
Hannah: well he's back at 6 and the banner's still on the floor
Priya: I've got icing on my hands I can't touch anything
Liam: someone hide the cake
Hannah: WHERE

Everybody stop shouting in capitals and breathe through your nose. Liam, banner up, two corners, wonky is fine, wonky is charming. Priya, you're not touching anything, so you're on lights, use your elbow. Hannah, cake goes in the oven. Not on, in. Ovens are where cakes are expected to be, nobody walking into a house ever opens one. How long have we got?

Hannah: he's at the gate
Liam: banner's up but it says HAPPY BIRTHDA because the Y fell off
Priya: lights are off
Hannah: why is he just standing there
Liam: he's on the phone

A man on the phone at his own gate is a man who's been given thirty seconds of grace by the universe. Liam, the Y. Find it. If you can't find it, a Y is three bits of tape, get creative. Everyone else away from the windows, he will see heads, heads are a dead giveaway. Hannah, who's he on the phone to?

Hannah: oh god he's on the phone to ME
Hannah: what do I do
Priya: DON'T ANSWER
Liam: ANSWER or he'll know something's up

Answer it. Calm voice, slightly bored, the voice of a woman watching telly. Tell him you're at your sister's. If there's background noise, she's got the radio on. Priya, mouth shut, I can hear you breathing from here. Do it now.

Hannah: ok he bought it
Hannah: he said he's popping to the shop first because we're out of milk
Liam: that's perfect that gives us like 10 mins
Priya: can I wash my hands now

Priya, wash your hands, you've earned it. Liam, that's ten minutes to sort the Y and get people out of the kitchen, because that's the first place a man goes with a pint of milk. Hannah, take the cake out of the oven and for the love of everything make sure nobody's turned it on in the panic. Now positions, and when he opens that door I want proper volume. A surprise party with a quiet surprise is just a lot of people in a dark room looking guilty.

Liam: he's back. we did it. he cried a bit
Hannah: the cake is slightly warm
Priya: someone did turn the oven on
Liam: it was me i panicked

Liam, you heated a birthday cake in a moment of crisis and then told everyone. Honesty and incompetence in the same breath, that's rare. Call it a warm chocolate fondant and serve it with ice cream. The man cried, the banner held, nobody blew the cover. In this business you take that result and you don't ask questions.

Mum: Dad is carving this year
Dad: I'm not carving, I carved in 2022 and there was an incident
Aunt Sue: there was blood on the parsnips
Grandad: I'll carve
Mum: you're 91 and you've got the tremor

Nobody panic about the knife, we're going to treat this like any delicate operation, which is to say, we pick the right man and everyone else keeps their distance. Grandad, with respect, your carving days are behind you, you've earned your seat and you'll be served first. Dad, 2022 is history. What you lacked then wasn't skill, it was a sharp knife and people stood behind you asking if it was done yet. Who's got the sharp knife?

Mum: it's in the drawer
Aunt Sue: that knife is blunt Pam, it's been blunt since the millennium
Dad: see this is what happened last time
Grandad: I've got a steel in my coat

Grandad, of course you have, a man of your generation travels prepared. Hand the steel to Dad. Dad, twenty strokes each side, nice and easy, then let the meat rest ten minutes while you do it, because a joint carved straight out of the oven fights back. Sue, you're on parsnips, keep them well out of range.

Dad: ok it's carving lovely actually
Mum: why are you cutting it so thick
Aunt Sue: that's a slab Graham that's not a slice
Dad: I'm getting heckled

Graham, ignore them, you're doing beautifully, that's what success sounds like in this family. Across the grain, a touch thinner, and let the knife do the work, don't saw at it like you're trying to get out of a shed. Pam, Sue, he can't carve and listen to a review at the same time. Go and make the gravy and leave the man to his art.

Grandad: gravy's lumpy
Mum: it's not lumpy it's rustic
Aunt Sue: it's lumpy

Sieve. Through a sieve into the jug, thirty seconds, problem gone and nobody need ever speak of it. Pam, rustic is something you say about a farmhouse, not a sauce. Now everyone sit down, Grandad gets the first plate, and anyone who brings up the parsnips of 2022 is on washing up.

Kofi: who's in goal tonight
Ryan: not me I went in last week
Sam: I've got a bad wrist
Kofi: you had a bad wrist last month
Sam: it's the same wrist
Jake: I'll go in if I can come out at half

Jake, step forward, you're the only one who's volunteered for anything without attaching a medical history. Half in goal, half out. Now Sam, you've had a bad wrist for a month, which means it's either a serious injury that needs a doctor or a very convenient one that only flares up near a goalpost. Which is it?

Sam: it's a bit of both honestly
Ryan: lol
Kofi: so he goes in second half then
Sam: I didn't say that

You didn't have to, Sam. A bit of both means you can stand in a goal with your hands out. Nobody's asking for diving saves, they're asking for a body in the frame. Second half, you're in. Go easy on the wrist and use your feet. Kofi, sort the bibs.

Kofi: we don't have bibs, Ryan was meant to wash them
Ryan: I did wash them
Kofi: and?
Ryan: they're still in the machine. at mine. since tuesday

Ryan, you've turned bibs into a science experiment. Those will be growing their own personalities by now. Tonight: one team in dark tops, one team in light, and Ryan, you're on the dark team because you've got a dark secret in your washing machine. When you get home, rewash them with a cup of white vinegar in the drum, then hang them out. Not tomorrow. Tonight.

Jake: what if the other team is all in grey tho
Kofi: then we're done for
Sam: shirts vs skins
Ryan: absolutely not it's November

Nobody's going skins, Sam, it's ten degrees and some of you have been on a festive diet since October. If it's grey on grey, you turn your tops inside out on one side, the seams'll tell you who's who. Problem solved. Now get to the pitch, warm up properly, and Kofi, for the record, the next person who says 'not me' to goal gets volunteered for the whole of next week.

Ellie: house meeting. bins. now.
Tom: it's not my week
Aisha: it's literally been nobody's week for three weeks
Tom: the rota was on the fridge
Ellie: the rota fell off the fridge in September
Tom: so technically there is no rota

Tom, 'technically there is no rota' is what a man says right before he becomes the rota. Three weeks of nobody's week means three weeks of everyone's rubbish fermenting in a cupboard and plotting against you. Ellie, Aisha, here's the fix: new rota, but this time it's a shared reminder on your phones, not a bit of paper clinging to a magnet for dear life. Tom starts. Tonight. Not because I'm cross, but because he raised the technicality and that's the price of a technicality.

Tom: that's not fair
Aisha: it's extremely fair
Ellie: Tom it's leaking
Tom: ok fine but who has next week

Aisha next week, then Ellie, then back round. Tom, it's leaking, which means you're carrying it at arm's length and you're giving the inside of that bin a rinse after, because it'll smell like a crime scene otherwise. Bin day comes back round every week whether you like it or not. That's the one appointment in this house that never cancels.

Dave: we're lost
Priya: we are NOT lost
Dave: the sat nav said left
Priya: the sat nav also tried to send us into a lake in Wales
Mo: can we stop at a services i'm dying
Dave: there IS no services we're in a field

Mo, you'll live, men have survived longer without a Greggs. Dave, the sat nav said left and you went left, and now you're in a field, so the sat nav has had its chance. Priya, you're right, you're not lost, you're just somewhere you didn't plan to be, which is how every good story starts. Here's the drill: Priya, open your phone map, not the sat nav, and find the nearest proper road. Head there, then take it from the top. Mo, first services you see, we're stopping, and Dave's buying, as penance for trusting a box that hates Wales.

Gemma: right so the hen do is gonna be about £450 each
Laura: FOUR HUNDRED AND FIFTY
Zara: I thought we said £200 max
Gemma: that was before the cocktail masterclass and the spa
Laura: and what else
Gemma: there's a lady who comes and does a sort of interpretive dance

Gemma, you've taken a two-hundred-quid budget and fed it after midnight. It's grown legs and a spa membership. Laura, Zara, deep breath. Gemma, I need to know one thing: who asked for the interpretive dance? Was it the bride, or was it you?

Gemma: it was sort of me
Zara: I KNEW IT
Laura: why would anyone want that
Gemma: it's very moving apparently

Moving it may be, Gemma, but it's moving two hundred and fifty quid out of everyone's pockets. The dance goes. Keep either the spa or the cocktails, not both. Cocktails are cheaper and more fun, spa days are just very expensive naps. You'll land around two hundred and thirty, which is close enough to the agreement that Zara can stop sharpening her knives.

Zara: I'm fine with 230
Laura: same
Gemma: can I at least do a little dance myself then
Laura: no

Gemma, you can dance all you like, as long as it's free and it's after the third cocktail when nobody's taking notes. That's the deal. Now send the new costing round before anybody books something else with feelings attached.

Ian: so who's got who for secret santa
Carol: you're not supposed to SAY Ian
Ian: I'm just asking generally
Paul: I got myself
Carol: then you put it back Paul!!
Paul: I'm not getting myself another gift, I'll just get myself something I want

Paul, buying yourself a present at the office do and calling it Secret Santa is not a loophole, it's a confession. Back in the hat, draw again. Ian, you've asked who's got who three different ways now, you're not 'asking generally', you're running a reconnaissance mission and everyone can see you doing it. Carol, keep the hat, you're the only one in this office who understands the word 'secret'. Ten pound limit, no exceptions, and nobody buys anyone a mug that says something about Mondays.

Rob: so there's three best men and one speech
Si: I think I should do most of it
Nathan: why
Si: I've known him longest
Nathan: you met him at uni. I met him in Year 7
Rob: I'm his brother. I've known him since he was born

Seniority's been settled, I think. Rob wins on account of being there when he arrived, unless anyone can top that. But that's not how you split a speech. You split it by who's good at what. Who's funny, who can get through a sentence without crying, and who's got the stories that can be told in front of his new mother-in-law?

Si: I'm funny
Nathan: Si you're not funny you're loud
Rob: I will 100% cry
Nathan: I've got good stories but most of them have the police in

Wonderful. A loud one, a crier, and a man with a criminal archive. Right then. Rob, you open and you close. One minute each, the heartfelt brother bit. If you go, you go, people expect the brother to well up. Nathan, the middle, the childhood stories, but only the ones where the police arrive and leave smiling. Si, you get the uni years, and loud works brilliantly if it's short. Three minutes, no more.

Si: three minutes is nothing
Nathan: three minutes of Si is an eternity
Rob: what about the bit about his ex

Nobody does the bit about his ex. Not a joke, not a hint, not a meaningful pause where everyone looks at Table Six. That's not a speech, it's a hand grenade with a ribbon round it. Si, three minutes is plenty, the best men always think the room wants more and the room never does. They want to laugh twice, cry once, and get to the cake.

Nathan: ok but who does the toast
Si: me
Rob: me
Nathan: I'll fight you both

The toast goes to Rob, being the brother and the closer. Nathan, put the fists away, you'll need both hands to hold the cards. Si, you get the last laugh line right before Rob takes over, and that's the best seat in the house. Get together Thursday, read it aloud, time it with a phone, and cut anything that only makes sense if you were there.

Ben: the sofa is stuck
Callum: it's not stuck it's wedged
Ben: what's the difference
Callum: wedged is temporary
Freya: it's been wedged for 25 minutes
Ben: I can't feel my left hand

Ben, put the sofa down. Gently. A man who can't feel his hand is a man about to drop something expensive on Callum. Callum, wedged that's been wedged for twenty-five minutes has been promoted to stuck. Freya, where exactly is it? Top of the stairs, bottom, or halfway, in the bit where every sofa in history goes to die?

Freya: halfway. at the turn in the stairs
Callum: the arm's caught on the bannister
Ben: I said we should've taken the legs off
Callum: the legs don't come off
Ben: everything's legs come off

Not everything's legs come off, Ben, but most sofas' do, so let's find out. Freya, you're smallest, can you see underneath? Look at where the leg meets the frame. If there's a bolt or it looks like it screws in, it's coming off. Callum, hold it steady and don't do anything clever.

Freya: they screw off!!!
Ben: I SAID
Callum: ok fine you said
Freya: three are off, the fourth is stuck against the wall

Victory has a smell and it smells like Ben being right. Leave the fourth for now. Callum, tip the whole thing up on its end, back of the sofa against the wall, so it's standing upright like a guardsman. Upright, a sofa takes up half the room it does flat. Then pivot it round the turn, arm first. Ben, you're at the bottom guiding, not lifting, your hand's had enough excitement.

Callum: it's upright
Callum: it's moving
Freya: mind the light switch
Callum: what light switch
Freya: that one

Callum, the light switch you've just put a sofa through is now a design feature. It's a fiver from any hardware shop and a ten-minute job with the power off at the board, so don't let anyone tell you that's a tragedy. Is the sofa through the turn or did we lose a soldier for nothing?

Ben: it's through!!
Freya: it's in the living room
Callum: it doesn't fit through the living room door
Ben: you're joking

Measure the door. Measure the sofa at its thinnest, which is usually from the back to the front of the seat, not across. If it's within a couple of inches, the living room door comes off its hinges. Three pins, pop them out with a screwdriver and a tap from below. Freya's on the screwdriver, she's got the best track record of the afternoon. Callum makes the tea. Ben sits on the stairs and gets the feeling back in his hand like the war hero he is.

Leah: guys the airbnb is in Porto not Lisbon
Kyle: what do you mean in Porto
Leah: like the address is Porto
Nadia: who booked it
Kyle: I booked it
Nadia: KYLE
Kyle: it said Portugal!!

Kyle, Portugal is a country, not an address. You've booked us a lovely flat three hours up the coast from where everyone's flights land. First things first: Leah, when's check-in, and what's the cancellation policy say? Don't argue, just read it out.

Leah: free cancellation until 48 hours before
Nadia: we fly in 5 days
Kyle: so we're fine?
Nadia: you're not fine you're on probation

Kyle, you're fine, and Nadia's right, you're on probation. Cancel the Porto one tonight, not tomorrow, tonight, and screenshot the confirmation. Leah, you find the new place in Lisbon, Kyle pays the deposit as a gesture of remorse. And for the record, from now on, nobody books anything without putting the full address in the chat first. One map pin. That's all it would've taken.

Jess: that's definitely a llama
Marco: alpaca
Jess: llama
Greg: could be a goat with a long neck
Marco: greg it's not a goat
Jess: we have 30 seconds

Greg, goats don't come with that neck. That's a camelid, and it's got the big upright banana ears, longer face, and it's well taller than the bloke next to it. That's a llama. Alpacas are smaller, fluffier, with a face like a disappointed teddy bear. Jess, write llama, and Greg, you're off the animal questions for the rest of the night.

Chloe: mum's 60th. ideas. go
Dan: restaurant
Jordan: we did a restaurant for her 50th
Dan: and it was nice
Jordan: it was a Harvester Dan
Chloe: can we try and do something nice this time

A woman's sixtieth deserves more than an unlimited salad bar and a balloon tied to the chair, Dan. No disrespect to the Harvester, it's done its service. Before I suggest anything, what does your mum actually like? Not what you'd like her to like. What she does on a Sunday when nobody's watching.

Chloe: gardening
Jordan: musicals. she knows every word of Les Mis
Dan: gin
Chloe: and she always says she wants to go to Kew

Gardens, gin, and singing her heart out. You've just planned it yourselves. Kew Gardens by day, there's usually something seasonal on, then a West End show in the evening, and a gin bar after where she's allowed to do the songs again without anyone shushing her. Split three ways it's very doable. Chloe, you organise. Jordan, tickets. Dan, you're on transport, and you're allowed one opinion, which is about which gin.

Dan: can it be a surprise
Chloe: she hates surprises
Jordan: she cried at the last one and not in a good way

Then it's not a surprise, Dan, it's an announcement with a nice card. Tell her the date, tell her to wear comfortable shoes and something she'd be happy to be photographed in. Let her look forward to it. Anticipation's half the present, and nobody's mum wants to be ambushed at sixty.

Lou: where is Stevie
Matt: he said he's 10 mins away
Lou: he said that 40 mins ago
Craig: I think he's at the bookies
Matt: why would he be at the bookies
Craig: because he's always at the bookies

Forty minutes and a sighting at a betting shop. A drummer running late is tradition, but he's doubling down. Lou, Matt, Craig, you can't sit there tuning the same string waiting for a man who's putting his rehearsal money on a dog. Run the set without drums. Matt, tap the kick on the floor with your foot. Do the vocal harmonies, the bits you never bother rehearsing because the drums drown them out.

Craig: he's just texted. says the dog came in. he's buying pizza
Lou: I'm still annoyed
Matt: I'm less annoyed

Pizza's an apology, Lou, it's just one that comes in a box. Take it and the slice. But when he walks in, he does the first song with no warm-up, as a matter of principle. And somebody tell him rehearsal's at seven, not 'at seven or whenever the four-forty at Romford finishes'.

Hamza: the code is 4 digits
Rach: we've got the clock, the painting and the dead plant
Oli: the dead plant isn't a clue it's just a dead plant
Hamza: everything's a clue in here
Rach: 11 minutes left
Oli: I've been pressing 1234 every so often just in case

Oli, stop pressing 1234, if that's the code, the people who built this room should be ashamed of themselves. Hamza, everything is a clue, but some clues are louder than others. What time does the clock say? And Rach, what's in the painting? Count things. Escape rooms love counting.

Hamza: clock is stopped at 7:15
Rach: painting has 3 ships and like 8 birds
Oli: the plant has 6 leaves
Oli: dead ones

Look at that. Oli, the dead plant you said wasn't a clue has given us a number. Seven, fifteen, three, eight, six. That's too many digits. Clock's probably two of them on its own. Try 7-1-5 with either the ships or the birds. Hamza, try 7153. If no, 7158. Oli, hands off the keypad.

Hamza: 7153 nothing
Hamza: 7158 nothing
Rach: what about the leaves
Oli: 7156??

Go on then, Oli, the plant's earned its moment. Seven one five six. If that opens it, you're never allowed to say 'it's just a dead plant' again as long as you live. If it doesn't, stop guessing and look for which order the room wants, ships before clock, birds after, there'll be a hint somewhere. Six minutes. Go.

Fiona: so what did everyone think of the book
Karen: loved it
Fiona: what was your favourite part
Karen: the... ending
Jo: I didn't finish it
Ann: I didn't start it
Karen: honestly I watched the trailer for the film

Karen, a trailer is not the book, it's the book in a hurry and wearing someone else's face. Ann, Jo, at least you were honest. Fiona, here's the truth: you're the only one who's read it, and that's not book club, that's a lecture. So tell them the story. Ten minutes, best bits, no spoilers. Next month, pick something shorter, and everyone emails one line about it before the meeting or they bring the wine. Shame's a great motivator, especially with a bottle of Pinot riding on it.

Sophie: who packed the tent pegs
Alex: I thought you did
Sophie: I packed the tent
Max: the tent comes with pegs
Sophie: it came with pegs in 2017
Alex: it's getting dark

So the pegs are a memory from 2017, wonderful. Sophie, Alex, Max, nobody's sleeping in a car tonight. What's the ground like, and what's around you? Rocks, sticks, a campsite shop, a man in a caravan who looks like he owns a hammer?

Max: there's loads of sticks
Alex: there's a shop but it shuts in 10 mins
Sophie: the ground's quite soft

Alex, run. Not jog. Run. Ask for tent pegs, and if they don't have them, buy a pack of skewers or a bag of the biggest nails they've got. Max, meanwhile, find sticks thick as your thumb, a hand-length long, and sharpen one end on a rock. Soft ground holds sticks fine if you angle them at forty-five degrees, pointing away from the tent. Sophie, get the tent laid out so the second the pegs arrive, you're in business.

Alex: got pegs!! last pack
Max: I've made 9 sticks
Sophie: we're up
Max: can we still use my sticks

Max, your sticks go on the guy ropes, that's honest work for a hand-carved peg. You've built a tent with your bare hands and a corner shop in the dark. Make a list on your phone tonight titled PEGS and never delete it.

Josh: who ate my cheese
Megan: what cheese
Josh: the expensive one. the one I was saving
Ruby: there was cheese?
Megan: oh the one with the wax on
Josh: SO YOU KNEW ABOUT IT
Megan: I know about lots of cheeses Josh

Megan, 'I know about lots of cheeses' is the most suspicious sentence ever spoken in a shared kitchen. Ruby, you're clear, nobody who says 'there was cheese?' in that tone of voice has eaten it. Josh, as for saving fancy cheese in a shared fridge, that's like leaving your wallet on a pub table and going for a smoke. It was always going to end in tears. Megan, you replace it, Josh, you get a shelf with your name on it, and next time it's in a box at the back behind the kale, where no thief ever looks.

Will: we need a team name for the league
Andy: Real Ale Madrid
Will: taken
Kai: Inter Yermum
Will: we're not putting that on the league website Kai
Andy: Borussia Teeth

Lads, every Sunday league team in Britain has already done the beer puns and the mum jokes. You need something nobody else has. What've you got that's yours? Where'd you meet, what's the pub, what's the thing you're terrible at?

Will: we all met at a pottery class tbh
Kai: we're terrible at heading the ball
Andy: the pub's called The Anchor

Then it's Atlético Kiln, hands down. A team that met at pottery and can't head a ball should own it and fire it in the kiln like a vase. And the pub can sponsor the shirts with an anchor on the front. Kai, you get to design the crest, but if there's anything rude hidden in it I'll find it.

Anna: bill's £312 for 6 so £52 each
Raj: I had a salad and tap water
Luke: you had three of my chips
Raj: three chips is not £52
Ciara: I didn't drink
Luke: you had the cocktail
Ciara: one cocktail

Pens down, everyone. Anna, splitting it evenly is lovely in theory, but in practice you've got a salad and a tap water being asked to fund someone's surf and turf. Raj's three chips were a sample, not a meal, Luke, no court in the land would convict. Who had the expensive stuff? Be honest, the receipt already knows.

Luke: I might have had the steak
Anna: and the wine was mostly me and Luke tbh
Theo: I had the steak too
Ciara: Theo's been quiet
Theo: I'm always quiet

Theo, quiet men eat steak too, the receipt doesn't care how loud you were. Here's the clean way: Raj and Ciara pay for what they had, plus a fair whack of the tip. Everyone else splits the rest. Anna, read me Raj's and Ciara's bits off the receipt.

Anna: Raj salad £12 water free. Ciara pasta £15 plus cocktail £11
Anna: so £12 and £26
Raj: plus tip
Ciara: plus tip yeah fine

Lovely. Call it fifteen percent on each, so Raj is fourteen, Ciara thirty. That's forty-four between them. Three hundred and twelve minus forty-four leaves two-sixty-eight between four of you, which is sixty-seven each. Luke, Theo, Anna, and whoever's the sixth person who hasn't said a word yet, I can count, there's six of you.

Anna: that's Mel, she's in the loo
Luke: Mel had the lobster
Anna: oh god

Of course she did. The one person not at the table to defend herself had the most expensive thing on the menu. Mel pays for the lobster on its own, the rest of you take whatever's left and split it four ways. Anna, you'll have to redo the sum, I'm not doing long division for a crustacean. And someone tell Mel before she comes back and offers to 'just split it evenly'.

Mum: so who's hosting Christmas
Sister: not me I did it last year
Brother: I've only got a two-bed
Mum: I can't, the kitchen's being done
Sister: you said the kitchen would be done by October
Mum: the builder's gone to Spain

A builder in Spain in November is a man who isn't coming back till the swallows do. So Mum's out. The sister did last year, she's done her shift. Which leaves the brother and his two-bed. How many are coming?

Mum: 9 with the kids
Brother: 9 people in my flat??
Sister: we fit 11 in mine and I've got a one-bath
Brother: fine but I'm not cooking a whole turkey

Nobody said you had to cook the whole turkey. Mum does the turkey at hers in an oven that, God willing, still works, and brings it over carved and foiled. Sister does the pudding and the starters. Brother, your job is roast potatoes, veg, gravy and making room for nine. Kids eat on the floor, that's Christmas law, they prefer it. Spread the work, keep the peace, and nobody ring the builder on Boxing Day, you'll only upset yourselves.

Gaz: the trade was fair
Pete: you gave Mitch a striker with a broken leg for his best midfielder
Gaz: he didn't ask about the leg
Mitch: I didn't KNOW about the leg
Gaz: it's on the internet Mitch
Pete: I'm the commissioner and I'm vetoing it

Gaz, 'it's on the internet' is what a fella says right after he sells you a car with no engine. Technically true, morally a crime. Mitch, you should've checked, but there's a code in fantasy leagues the same as in any honest business: you don't flog injured goods to your mates. Pete, you're the commissioner, does your league have a veto rule written down anywhere?

Pete: kind of. we said 'no dodgy trades' in the group chat in August
Gaz: that's not a rule that's a vibe
Mitch: it's a rule

It's a rule now, because I'm making it one. Pete, write it down properly: any trade can be vetoed by majority vote within twenty-four hours. Then put this one to a vote. My guess is it'll go about four to one, with Gaz on the losing side. Gaz, you're a shrewd operator, I'll give you that. Next time, use it on the people in your other league.

DM (Sarah): ok you're at the door of the dragon's lair. what do you do
Tim: I attack the door
Leon: you can't attack a door
Tim: I'm a barbarian I can attack anything
Nell: can we maybe check for traps first
Tim: traps are for cowards

Tim, a barbarian can attack anything, and that's exactly how barbarians end up as a cautionary tale carved over a dragon's doorway. Nell's right, a door outside a dragon's lair is not a door, it's a question. Sarah's the DM, so Sarah, can Nell roll for traps before the big man puts his axe through the architecture?

DM (Sarah): sure, Nell roll perception
Nell: 17
DM (Sarah): you notice a pressure plate right in front of the door
Tim: ok so I attack the pressure plate
Leon: TIM

Tim, you're the type to hear 'don't touch the red button' and take it as a dare. Leon, hold him back. Nell, you're the brains of this outfit, so you call the play. Does anyone have anything that can disarm it? A rogue, a long stick, a spell, a lad from the last village you can send in first?

Leon: I'm a wizard I've got mage hand
Nell: can mage hand press the plate from a distance
DM (Sarah): yes
Tim: boring
Leon: we press it from 30ft away and see what happens

Lovely work. That's how professionals take a door. Leon, you stand thirty feet back, Nell behind you, and Tim, you get the job you were born for: standing at a safe distance holding your axe, ready to hit whatever comes out. Sarah, roll your dice, what happens?

DM (Sarah): a massive spiked log swings down where the door would've been
Nell: ha
Leon: TIM
Tim: ok fine that would've hurt
Tim: can I attack the log now

Tim, the log is defeated, it's swung, it's spent, it's a log having a lie down. But I'll tell you what, the door's still shut. You've been begging all night to hit something. Go on. Barbarian versus the door. That's the moment you've been waiting for, and it's safe now, thanks to the other two doing all the thinking for you.

Tim: I rolled a natural 20
DM (Sarah): the door explodes inward in a shower of splinters. the dragon wakes up
Nell: oh no
Leon: TIM

There it is. Every party has one, and yours rolled a twenty to prove it. Look at the bright side: you wanted a fight, now you've got the biggest one in the building. Nell, Leon, scatter, get behind something. Tim, you woke it, you stand in front of it. That's not punishment, that's poetry.

Brenda: someone's been taking my courgettes
Keith: nobody wants your courgettes Brenda you've got a glut
Brenda: that's not the point
Geoff: it might be foxes
Brenda: foxes don't take courgettes in a carrier bag Geoff
Geoff, foxes are opportunists, but they've never once shopped with a carrier bag. That's a two-legged thief. Brenda, how many have gone, and when do you notice?

Brenda: five or six a week. always gone by Monday
Keith: so the weekend
Geoff: Derek's only here on Sundays
Keith: Derek doesn't even grow courgettes
Brenda: EXACTLY

Interesting. A man who doesn't grow courgettes and only turns up when the gates are quiet. That's not proof, it's a pattern. Keith, Geoff, nobody marches up to Derek with a pitchfork. Brenda, here's the elegant version: put a sign on your plot. 'Free courgettes, help yourself, just ask.' If they still vanish in silence, you've got a thief. If Derek asks, you've got a man who likes courgettes and is too proud to say so, and that's not a crime, that's a man in need of a recipe.

Keith: can we put up a camera
Geoff: the committee will never approve a camera
Brenda: I'll put the sign up

Wise choice, Brenda. Cameras on allotments start wars that outlast everyone in them. A sign and a smile, and if Derek's the culprit, he'll either confess or start leaving you jam as an apology. Either way, you'll eat well.

Nina: who's driving to the festival
Zac: not me I'm planning on being unwell
Nina: unwell how
Zac: festival unwell
Phoebe: I don't have a licence
Ollie: I'll drive there but not back
Nina: that's not how cars work Ollie

Ollie's spotted the flaw nobody wants to say out loud: someone's driving home on Monday morning feeling like a dropped kebab. Here's the plan. Nina, you drive there, Ollie drives back, Zac pays for both lots of petrol because 'festival unwell' sounds like it costs a fortune and he can afford to fund the transport. Phoebe, you're DJ and snacks, both directions. Ollie, you stay dry on Sunday night, and I mean Sunday afternoon onwards, because the morning after doesn't care how good you feel at midnight.

Priyanka: presentation is tomorrow at 9 and we have 4 slides
Chris: I did my bit
Priyanka: your bit is a title slide chris
Maya: I've been ill
Jack: I thought it was next week
Priyanka: I'm going to scream

Priyanka, scream once, into a pillow, then come back. We've got a night, four people and four slides, and that's not hopeless, it's a heist on a tight clock. How many slides should it be, how long is it meant to run, and what's the topic?

Priyanka: 12 slides, 15 mins, renewable energy policy in the EU
Maya: I can do research I'm feeling better
Jack: I can do the design
Chris: I'll do the conclusion

Now we're moving. Twelve slides, three sections, three slides each, plus title, intro and conclusion. Priyanka, you write the intro and the structure tonight and send it to the chat by eight, because you clearly know what it's meant to say. Maya, the evidence: a slide on wind, one on solar, one on targets for 2030. Jack, a clean template plus the three slides on member states. Chris, the conclusion and the references, and you're presenting first, because a man who's only done the title slide talks first while he's still got the excuse of nerves. Everything into a shared deck by midnight, run-through at eight. No 'I thought it was next week', Jack.

Ade: the cake has been delivered
Seema: great where is it
Ade: number 14
Seema: we live at number 41
Ade: oh
Kwame: who lives at 14
Ade: no idea
Seema: the party is in an hour

Ade, you've transposed two numbers and sent a birthday cake to a stranger. It's not ideal, but it's not lost, it's just being looked after by someone who didn't order it. Number fourteen is on the same street, yes? Somebody needs to knock, and it shouldn't be Ade, because he'll look like a man who's come to apologise for something.

Kwame: I'll go
Seema: take a card or something
Kwame: I'm not taking a card to get my own cake back
Ade: it's got her name on it, they can't argue

Ade's right, a cake that says 'Happy Birthday Lola' in icing is not getting stolen by somebody called Brian. Kwame, go, be charming, say there's been a delivery mix-up, and if they've already opened the box, offer them a slice. Nothing calms a stranger like being allowed to keep a piece of the evidence.

Kwame: they've had a bit
Seema: WHAT
Kwame: like a corner. they thought it was from their nan

Of course they did. Somebody's nan sends cake out of the blue, you don't ask questions, you get a fork. Seema, a corner missing is fixable. Turn the cake so the bite faces the wall, or, if it's a big chunk, slap a candle and some fruit in the gap and call it artistic. Kwame, bring it home level, both hands, don't take any shortcuts over walls.

Kwame: it's home
Seema: I put strawberries in the hole
Ade: it looks better than before honestly
Seema: don't push it Ade

Ade, take the compliment on behalf of fate and say nothing else for the rest of the evening. Seema, that's a rescue. Lola will never know, and number fourteen have a lovely story about the nan who didn't send a cake. Everybody won.

Uncle Phil: we need to clear Dad's shed this weekend
Cousin Becky: I want the toolbox
Cousin Aaron: I was gonna ask for the toolbox
Uncle Phil: there's like 200 tins of screws in there
Becky: he labelled everything, I want to keep the labels
Aaron: you want to keep the LABELS?

Aaron, you're about to argue with a woman who wants to preserve a dead man's handwriting. You will lose that argument, and you should. Phil, before anyone fights over anything, was there anything your dad said about who gets what? A note, a will, even a passing comment over a cup of tea?

Uncle Phil: he said the lathe goes to whoever would use it
Becky: I've never used a lathe
Aaron: I have
Becky: fine, Aaron gets the lathe, I get the toolbox

There you go, sorted between yourselves like grown-ups, which would've made him proud. Aaron, lathe. Becky, toolbox and the labels. Phil, the tins of screws: keep the ones he labelled, offer the rest to a local men's shed or repair café, they'll treat them like treasure. And all of you take one small thing each that isn't valuable but is him. A pencil stub, a mug, the old radio. That's the stuff you'll actually keep.

Rhi: I'm doing Bohemian Rhapsody
Mal: you can't do it on your own it's 6 minutes
Rhi: watch me
Steph: I wanted to do it
Mal: nobody's doing it the queue's already 40 minutes
Steph: we could do it together
Rhi: I don't share Queen

Rhi, nobody owns Queen, not even Queen. Six minutes on your own is a hostage situation for everyone else in the bar. Steph, you're in. Split it: Rhi does the ballad bit and the bit at the end, Steph the opera bit, and Mal, you're doing the 'Galileo' backing vocals from the floor, because a song like that's a group effort or it's nothing. Get it in the queue now before someone's uncle puts down 'Mr Brightside' for the fourth time tonight.

Danny: it's Oasis
Meera: it's Blur
Danny: it's obviously Oasis listen to the guitar
Frank: it might be the Verve
Meera: Frank you say the Verve for everything
Frank: and one day I'll be right

Frank, a stopped clock is right twice a day, but it doesn't get a point for it in a pub quiz. Danny, Meera, the Oasis versus Blur war ended decades ago and both sides lost their hair. What's the question exactly? Name the band, name the song, or name the year?

Meera: name the song AND band
Danny: it's the one that goes dun dun dunnnn
Meera: that's every song Danny

Danny, 'dun dun dunnnn' is the musical equivalent of describing a suspect as 'a bloke'. Here's how you settle it without coming to blows. Whoever can sing the next line of the chorus, out loud, right now, in front of the whole table, gets to write the answer. If you both can, that's a two-way tie and Frank's the tiebreak, and for once the Verve's got nothing to do with it.

Sana: so Jamie's boyfriend basically lives here now
Jamie: he doesn't live here
Oscar: he has a toothbrush, a drawer, and a parcel delivered here last week
Jamie: that was a one-off
Sana: it was a wardrobe Jamie
Jamie: a SMALL wardrobe

Jamie, a man who has wardrobes delivered to a flat lives at that flat. That's not my opinion, that's furniture law. But nobody's in trouble yet. Sana, Oscar, what's actually bothering you? The rent, the bathroom, the hot water, or just the presence of a tall man in the kitchen at seven in the morning?

Oscar: bills mainly. he showers like he's in a car wash
Sana: and the bathroom queue
Jamie: he could chip in I guess

There's the deal, Jamie, and you've found it yourself. Anyone staying more than four nights a week chips in on bills, let's say a quarter of the utilities, since he's effectively the fourth flatmate. Oscar, you'll get your hot water back, or at least someone's paying for it. Sana, set up a bathroom slot system in the mornings. Jamie, you have the chat with him, not the group, because nobody wants their boyfriend being negotiated with by a committee.

Jamie: he's said yes
Oscar: great
Sana: tell him the wardrobe stays in your room

And there's the last clause, Sana, beautifully drafted. Wardrobe in Jamie's room, bills split four ways, bathroom on a schedule. That's peace in our time. Put it in writing in the group chat so in six months nobody can say they didn't agree.

Lewis: shirts arrived
Paddy: and?
Lewis: they say 'STEVE'S LAST NIGHT OF FREEDUM'
Paddy: freedum
Greg: who proofread it
Lewis: I did
Greg: so nobody

Freedum. Lewis, you've given a stag do a shirt that looks like it's been written by the groom's nephew. Greg, easy with the knife, the man's already bleeding. Lewis, how many shirts and when's the stag?

Lewis: 12 shirts. stag is saturday
Paddy: that's 3 days
Greg: can we get them reprinted
Lewis: they took 2 weeks

Then reprinting's off the table. Two options. One, a fabric marker, cross out the U, write an O above it with a little arrow, like an editor's correction. Two, lean in completely. FREEDUM becomes a deliberate joke, and you make it Steve's fault somehow. Nobody's going to believe twelve shirts were misspelt by accident if you all wear them with a straight face.

Paddy: option two
Greg: how is it steve's fault though
Lewis: steve can't spell, he wrote 'definately' in his best man speech for Dan

Then the story writes itself. On the back of each shirt, in marker: 'SPELT BY STEVE'. Lewis gets off, Steve's the joke, and everybody understands it by the second pint. Greg, you're on markers, get the thick permanent ones, not felt tips that run in the rain.

Greg: done. got 12
Lewis: I feel like I got away with it
Paddy: you did not get away with it, you're buying the first round

Paddy's right, Lewis, you didn't get away with it, you got a sentence reduced on appeal. First round's yours. That's the cheapest way out of a typo in human history. Have a good Saturday, all of you, and nobody let Steve near a pen until he's back home.

Ella: you landed on Mayfair that's £2000
Noah: it's not £2000
Ella: it's with hotels Noah
Noah: when did you put hotels on
Ella: when you went to the loo
Lily: she did it while you were in the loo, I saw
Noah: that's CHEATING

Noah, I hate to be the one to tell you, but buying hotels while a man's in the loo is ruthless, it's not cheating. There's no rule saying the property market waits for anyone's bladder. Ella, I admire the timing. Lily, were the hotels paid for out of the bank properly, not borrowed from the free parking pot?

Lily: she paid. I watched
Noah: I can't afford £2000
Ella: then mortgage your stuff

Mortgage the lot, Noah, the stations first, they're your weakest earners. If that still doesn't cover it, you're out, and you go out with dignity, not by flipping the board. A flipped Monopoly board has ended more family relationships than any will reading. Ella, collect your money and try not to look smug, it's a long Christmas.

Dad: [voice note 4:37]
Dad: [voice note 3:12]
Katie: dad please just type
Sam: I'm not listening to 8 minutes of you in a car park
Dad: [voice note 0:04]
Katie: what did that one say
Sam: I think it was 'ok'

Katie, Sam, your dad's discovered a new toy and he's playing with it like a kid with a drum kit at Christmas. He's not going to stop on his own. Here's the deal, Dad, if you're reading this: voice notes are allowed, but under a minute, and never from a car park with the engine running. Anything over that, you type, or you ring like a civilised man. Katie, Sam, play the long ones on double speed in the meantime. Eight minutes becomes four, and your dad sounds like an auctioneer, which is a bonus.

Bride (Rosie): seating plan is a nightmare
Groom (Ash): just put people anywhere
Rosie: I can't put Auntie Val near Uncle Clive
Ash: why
Rosie: the caravan
Maid of honour (Jen): oh god the caravan
Ash: what caravan

Ash, there's always a caravan, every family's got one, and you're better off not knowing the details until you're legally part of this. Rosie, the golden rule: put the feud on opposite sides of the room, both facing the top table, neither facing each other. How many tables, and who else is a problem?

Rosie: 10 tables. Val and Clive. my mate Hollie and her ex who's also Ash's cousin
Jen: and Ash's friends who'll be loud
Ash: they're not that loud

Ash, everyone's friends are 'not that loud' until the third bottle. Back table near the bar, so they're happy and you're not distracted by them. Hollie and the ex, different sides, but give Hollie a table with her own mates so she's having a ball and not watching anyone. Val by the window on the left, Clive near the door on the right. Jen, you're on patrol, if Val starts walking towards Clive with intent, intercept her with a glass of fizz.

Jen: I can do that
Rosie: this is actually doable now
Ash: I still want to know about the caravan

Ash, ask Clive about the caravan on your first anniversary, at a family barbecue, from a safe distance. By then you'll be part of the furniture and he can't uninvite you. Today, you've got a wedding to get to the other side of.

Coach (Terry): 4-0 down at half. thoughts
Mack: their number 9 is a cheat
Dean: he's not a cheat he's just fast
Mack: he's fast and he's a cheat
Joe: we haven't touched the ball in 20 minutes
Terry: anyone else

Mack, the man is quick, that's not cheating, that's a gift from God and his mother. Joe's said the true thing here, twenty minutes without the ball. You can't score if you're watching the game from your own half like a spectator who's paid in. Terry, what's the shape you've been playing?

Terry: 2-2 with Joe floating
Dean: Joe's not floating he's just lost
Joe: I'm floating
Mack: their 9 is getting in behind us every time

Here's the fix, then. Mack, you're not marking the number nine anymore, you're dropping five yards deeper and letting him come to you. A fast man needs space to run into, so stop giving him any. Joe, you're not floating, you're anchored. Stay in front of the defence, every ball goes through you. Dean, Terry, you two press their keeper and centre-half when they've got it, make them kick it long and hurried.

Dean: and if they still score
Terry: then we lose 8-0 and go to the pub
Mack: I want to at least score one

Mack wants a goal. Good. That's the right attitude at four down. Forget the comeback, nobody turns four-nil round in twenty minutes of five-a-side. Set the target at winning the second half. Get one, then get another. Make their number nine earn every touch. The pub will still be there either way, but it's a far nicer pint when you've won the second half.

Terry: final score 6-3
Mack: I scored two
Joe: we won the second half 3-2
Dean: I'm counting that as a win

Dean, count it. Three-two in the second half against a team with a greyhound up front is a proper result. Mack, two goals, and you didn't call anyone a cheat for at least twenty minutes, that's growth. Joe, anchored, not floating. Keep that shape next week from the first whistle and you won't need to be rescued at half time.

Mrs Patel: we need to apply to the council for the road closure
Gary: I'll do it
Mrs Patel: you said that last year Gary
Gary: and I nearly did
Linda: we also need someone for the bouncy castle
Gary: I'll do that too
Linda: no.

Gary, a man who 'nearly did' last year's council form does not get handed a second job, let alone an inflatable one. Mrs Patel, you take the council application, it's usually online and they want it a good few weeks before the date, so do it this week. Linda, you're on the bouncy castle, get quotes and check they've got insurance. Gary, you're on bunting and tables, which is the job you can't nearly do, because everyone will see if it's not there. Lovely. That's a street party with a chain of command.

Ifeoma: the landlord said yes to a cat!!
Cal: we're calling it Gerald
Harriet: we are not calling a cat Gerald
Cal: why not
Harriet: because it's a girl
Cal: Geraldine then
Ifeoma: we haven't even picked the cat yet

Ifeoma, you've hit on the actual problem, they're naming a cat that doesn't exist. Cal, you've decided on a name before a face, and that's how a ginger beast ends up called something that doesn't suit it. Harriet, you're right about the gender, though I'd say any cat would carry Gerald with dignity. Go to the rescue, pick the cat, and let the cat's face decide. Shortlist: three names each, vote when you get home.

Cal: fine. but Gerald's on my shortlist
Harriet: so's Biscuit
Ifeoma: we're getting the black one with one eye btw I've decided

Ifeoma's gone and decided for all of you, which is how it should be, she's the one who asked the landlord. A one-eyed black cat is a creature of mystery and menace, and she does not deserve to be called Biscuit. Gerald might be in with a shout after all. Get a proper bed, a scratching post, and keep her in for two weeks while she learns the place is hers. Which it will be, by Friday.

Yusuf: we've got two screws left over
Bella: that's normal
Yusuf: and a whole door
Bella: that's less normal
Craig: the door's meant to go on last
Yusuf: Craig it's a wardrobe. it's all door

Two screws and a door left over. That's not a wardrobe, Yusuf, that's a cabinet with ambitions. Bella, Craig, stop building. Before anyone touches another piece, what step are you on, and does the thing currently stand up on its own?

Bella: step 14 of 22
Craig: it stands up
Yusuf: it leans
Bella: it leans a bit

If it leans, there's a back panel missing or a side's on backwards. Wardrobes stay square because of that flimsy board on the back that everyone thinks is decoration. Is the back panel on? And are all the little holes facing inwards, or have you got a side panel staring at the wall?

Craig: back panel's on
Yusuf: one side's got holes on the outside
Bella: oh no
Craig: that was me

Craig, honesty in a crisis. That's a quality, but you'll still be the one fixing it. Lie it flat on its back. Undo that side, flip it so the holes face in, and screw it back. Don't overtighten the cam locks, a quarter turn till it bites. Yusuf, hold it steady, Bella, read the next step out loud before anyone does anything.

Bella: ok it's square
Yusuf: it's standing straight
Craig: but there's still the two screws
Bella: step 17 uses two screws

Then they weren't spare, they were early. Everything's back on schedule. Step seventeen, Bella reads, Craig screws, Yusuf watches Craig like a man supervising a nephew with a power tool. Then the doors, and Craig, you were right, the doors do go on last, so that's one apiece.

Yusuf: doors are on. but one door is lower than the other
Craig: it's because I'm better than you
Bella: there's a little adjusting screw on the hinge

Bella's been carrying this operation since step one and she's just won the final round. Little screw on the hinge, a few turns at a time, you'll see the door rise. And Craig, you're not better than anyone, you put a wall on backwards. Stand it up against the wall, fix it to the wall with the bracket in the bag, because these things topple when they're full, and the three of you go and get a takeaway. Building furniture as a group and still talking afterwards is rarer than a set of instructions that makes sense.
